findings.description: The reports bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects (including the vendor roster) are stored with default S3-managed keys with no enforced encryption or KMS key control.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block and no account-level block is configured, leaving the bucket open to being made public (e.g. via a later policy or ACL change) with no defense in depth.
No logging block is configured, so access to this bucket (which contains vendor data) is not recorded; also this bucket is not a target of any other bucket's logging.

The seed object is uploaded without server_side_encryption or kms_key_id, so the vendor roster is written to S3 without customer-controlled encryption; it also has no source_hash/etag pinning so content can be replaced undetected.
The ledger bucket contains financial export data but has no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving the data encrypted only with S3-managed keys and not under KMS key control.
No public access block is applied to the ledger bucket, so it can be exposed via bucket policies or ACL changes without any account-level safeguard.
Access to the financial ledger exports is not logged and the bucket is not covered by any logging configuration, so unauthorized reads would go undetected.
Model artifacts are stored without server_side_encryption_configuration, so artifacts are not encrypted under a KMS key and cannot be protected with key-level access control.
No public access block is configured for the model artifacts bucket, allowing it to be exposed publicly through policies or ACL modifications.
Operational runbooks (which commonly contain credentials, endpoints and internal procedures) are stored with no server_side_encryption_configuration and no KMS key.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached to the runbooks bucket, so it can be made publicly readable without any account-level restriction.
The runbooks bucket has no logging block and is not a logging target, so reads of sensitive operational documentation are not audited.

Even the audit log bucket has no public access block; a public policy would let an attacker delete or tamper with audit evidence (logging to the bucket is also not enforced via a bucket policy requiring aws:SourceArn).

findings.issue_category: log delivery writes allowed via ACL
findings.description: The bucket uses the legacy acl = "log-delivery-write" grant, giving the S3 log delivery group write/read-ACP rights on the audit bucket instead of using a least-privilege bucket policy, which can be abused to overwrite or manipulate log objects.

Access logs for model artifacts are written to aws_s3_bucket.audit_trail, which is granted the legacy log-delivery-write ACL; log objects in the target bucket are not protected by an explicit policy restricting the source bucket.
